newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia's stock market set for further gains.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia's stock market set for further gains.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's stock market should post further gains this year based on buoyant domestic economic growth, attractive equity returns and the prospect of more outside funds, Saudi bankers and analysts said on Monday.

The market's all-share index, which tracks the exchange's 70 listed firms, has risen 6.5 percent since January when the government announced an expansionary budget and completed paying off debts to local contractors, suppliers and farmers.
"The bullish sentiment in the market is expected to prevail during the balance of this year," according to Henry Azzam, chief economist at Saudi Arabia's National Commercial Bank.

In the week to last Thursday the index, dominated by the banking stocks, rose to 163.17 points while trading volume jumped 101 percent to 688 million riyals ($183.4 million) due to expectations of further stock price rises.
The exchange, which has seen capitalisation from its six sectors soar to over 181 billion riyals, grew 11 percent in 1996, fanned by strong economic growth as a result of firm world oil prices.
Saudi Finance Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Asaf has forecast a real growth rate of nearly six percent in 1997 following a nominal growth rate of 8.6 percent last year.
Key to the exchange's performance will be its 11 listed banks that account for nearly 40 percent of capitalisation.

"The market offers the lowest price to earnings ratio in the region which makes it very attractive to investors," said Beshr Bakheet, managing partner at the Riyadh-based Bakheet Financial Advisors. He estimated the earning ratio at 12.

Investors in the exchange have also taken encouragement from first steps taken by the government to gradually open the exchange, which so far is limited to Saudi nationals and other Gulf Arabs, to international funds.

Saudi American Bank (SAMBA), 30 percent owned by Citibank, was given the green light in March to set up the first closed-end fund to allow foreign participation in the bourse which limits outside investment and has no market-makers.
"The new fund is considered to be an important step on the road towards opening the Saudi stock market to international capital," according to a report drawn up by Azzam.

"If (Saudi monetary agency) SAMA eventually permits each of the other 11 banks to establish such funds, the theoretical maximum combined size of the 12 funds would come to around 21.5 billion riyals...a significant amount."
Total share value traded in 1996 was 25.4 billion riyals.
"The stock exchange will see a growth trend because of the gradual opening of the market," said one Saudi-based banker who declined to be named.

Having mutual funds open to foreign investors is also seen a way of curing the market's narrow share ownership base and accelerating moves to improve company disclosure, protection against insider-dealing and boost turn-over.
Only two percent of the population invests in the market and more than a third of all shares remain in government hands.
It would also allow the exchange to tap into remittances, which Azzam estimates at an annual $17 billion, that the country's six million expatriates send home.
